utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever you're ready to start, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. Mr. Oric, are you receiving interpretation in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can hear the translation, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and good morning to the Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to everyone. My name is John Jones, co-counsel. I appear on behalf of Naser Oric with Jasmina Cosic, our lead assistant, and Geoff Roberts, our CaseMap manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones, and good morning to you and your team. Anything by way of preliminary before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Very short, Your Honour. To update you further regarding the schedule of witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- we provided a schedule on -- dated the 1st of March, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Number 39, that witness should be rescheduled as it included a projected date of the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And we would like to provide you and the other parties with a new schedule, and we plan to do that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Wubben. The rest stands, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. I thank you. So let's get the witness. I take it you're not going to take long, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope to conclude within a half hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge Tankic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make yourself comfortable. Take a seat please, and we are going to proceed with your testimony. You don't need to repeat the solemn declaration, and I don't need to explain to you that it still stands, of course. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tankic. Your Honours, prior to proceeding, I just wanted to correct the record. I understand that an ERN number was given yesterday that should be 03615766, and on the record it would have been -- I would have stated erroneously 03615767.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are right. I noticed that yesterday. And I think there was also something wrong in the record when it came to the corresponding page in English, whether it was 14 or 15. But in any case, leave it. I think we know exactly what you were referring to on this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to draw your attention to document with ERN number 03648890. The document is not in the annex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Sellers: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, I would ask you to look at this document, please. Are you familiar with this document, Mr. Tankic?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this document part of the archives of the High Prosecutor's Office in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give the original of this document to the Office of the Prosecutor during proofing and hence a photocopy was made from your original?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you then sign on the ERN page that concludes in 03648895? Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are my numbers and my signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please, then, inform the Trial Chamber, what were the circumstances of the content of the document that we have before us as it relates to the High Court or the district military court.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are criminal charges against members of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army from Srebrenica, charges raised by the security station in Srebrenica, so by the civilian police. And the charges were submitted to the higher prosecution in Tuzla in July 1993 for triple murder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would draw your attention to page 4 of the document in the English translation, please, and the lower part of that page which refers to enclosures or attachments to the document. Mr. Tankic, I would ask you now: Those enclosures that appear to include statements, official notes and other statements, is that normal and proper procedure when conducting an investigation that relates to charges of murder?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, this was pretrial procedure carried out by the police, so these are witnesses' statements and evidence, a drawing of the place where the murders were committed, videotape, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was the proper form or venue for this type of investigation and subsequent indictment/prosecution the High Court in Tuzla or the district military court in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These criminal charges arrived by mistake to the higher prosecution in Tuzla, and given the nature of the perpetrator, they were submitted to the district military prosecution in August 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask for a P number for this document and have it moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have arrived at P50 ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 7, Your Honour, P507.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being received -- tendered, received, admitted and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P507.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask that we look at annex page 17. The ERN number would be 03615771. The P number is 505.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber the reason for the content of this document.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a request by the -- by the district military prosecution to undertake an investigation against a member of the BiH army, sent to the investigating judge of the military court. This is the usual, normal form, where the prosecutor sends the request to the investigating judge to undertake an investigation against a person. The alleged crime here is murder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, I would ask you to turn to the last page of that document, and to draw your attention to the paragraph that's preceded by the sub-title "Statement of Reasons". Mr. Tankic, is the reason that this request originated, was it based upon information that came from the public security station in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this case, also the security station, Srebrenica, filed charges, and the district prosecutor acted accordingly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this document, from your knowledge, show that the district prosecutor's office was functioning during the armed conflict and that function included looking at investigative information from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would now like to move to another document. It's part of P505 and I understand it is under Page 9 of the annex, ERN number would be 03615762.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see the English -- in the English version it starts at the bottom of page 10 and continues on page 11. Correct me if I am wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it starts midway through page 9 and concludes on page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That wouldn't correspond with what we have, because on page 9 -- on page 9, if you look at more or less towards the middle of the page, just above the words "the public prosecutor's office Srebrenica", there is slash the page with ERN number 03615761A contains the following and handwritten entries, and an illegible signature, the date and then what as follows: If you go to the next page, as you approach the bottom of the page, about -- just above the last paragraph there, they have slash the next page 03615762A, contains only the letter -- only the date, et cetera. So I'm either missing 5762, which I don't see anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been informed that that's a mistake, the ERN number that appears midway through page 9 appears to precede the document, but that the ERN number for that document is found at the bottom of the document in the translation and that would be toward the bottom one-third of page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It states next page 03615762A.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we understand that actually the English translation pertains to 03615762, is what is above that number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I'll check. Oh, I see. I see. But anyway, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that you know which document you are referring the witness to, because I don't want any confusion. So let's try to sort this out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when we go to the original B/C/S document with the -- for those of us who have a very limited knowledge of the language, when we look at the document, we see that in the upper left-hand corner, about less than one-third, one quarter of the way down the page, there is a series of numbers that appear to be handwritten. If one would then look on page 9 of the annex, we see that that corresponds with that series of handwritten numbers 4.995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that basically means that on page 9 of the English version, at the end towards the end of the first half of that page, where we have the page with ERN number 03615761A, it should be 03615762.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour,.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's the only --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes Your Honour, I believe if there's been not a mistake in the translation of the number, the ERN number should be at the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. Not even. What's missing is -- that is correct because that refers to 5761A and 5761A indeed has the signature of the witness, I assume, plus the date of 9/9/2004. So what's missing is that between that two line paragraph or statement, and the next part where it says the public prosecutor's office, we should have an insertion there, the page with ERN number 5762 follows and then you start with the public prosecutor, because then 5762 is what we have following on page 9 of the English version. So what we have is, Ms. Sellers, after the word -- the paragraph, the page with ERN number 0361 contains the following handwritten entries and illegible signature and the date 9/9/2004, there should be a new paragraph saying: And the page with ERN number 03615762 contains the following letter, or dispatch or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree. Can we at least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, did you follow me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour. I do follow and in fact if it's of any assistance on page 10 of 22, before the words "I left Srebrenica as a displaced person", that's probably page 03615763 starting. That's at least the note that I've made. So it's the same observation that I believe you had that annotation it would be seen that the next page from the B/C/S follows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Again you still -- you have missing precisely another statement to the -- similar to the one I have just mentioned, yes. Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and defence counsel. Do we all see the correct B/C/S and English from which I will now ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, thank you for your patience. I would ask you to look at the document before you, the ERN number ending in 5762 and I would ask you, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain to the Trial Chamber the origin and the reason for the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was drafted by the Srebrenica prosecutor after arriving in Tuzla having been expelled in August, 1995. This was a common way to describe what she left behind in her office in Srebrenica, the sort of situation that prevailed. This was forwarded to the republican prosecutor in Sarajevo to the justice ministry of the Tuzla canton and of the federation as well as to the municipal board of Srebrenica municipality, which at the time was based in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, if you notice the last paragraph on the first page it starts with the public prosecutor's office in Srebrenica, started its work. I would like to draw your attention to that paragraph. And in particular, the second sentence where it says that the premises where the prosecutor's office used to work, the basic court building Srebrenica were inhabited by refugees who destroyed all the documents of the public prosecutor's office. Mr. Tankic the question I would like to ask you is that, if documents were destroyed from the public prosecutor's office, would those documents relate to documents that were prior to the arrival of the public prosecutor in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to the arrival, I assume these are prewar documents for the most part, belonging to the former prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, documents in the public prosecutor's office that would pertain to cases that should have been sent to the High Court in Tuzla, where you worked in 1992, would they have been part of the documents possibly destroyed?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That strikes me as less likely. I assume that the refugees had been on those premises right from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, I would like to ask that between September 1992 until June 1st 1993 when the Srebrenica public prosecutor arrived, where would have been the proper place for any persons who wanted to convey information to the military district prosecutor's office, where would have been a proper place for them to address themselves?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian or the military police in Srebrenica and they would then forward this to the civilian prosecutor until as late as September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would that also have been the practice between September 1992 until June 1st 1993 when the civilian prosecutor arrived?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time it was possible also to file a report with the civilian prosecutor in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would be after June 1993?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 1st of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this -- this document is already into evidence. I would like to move to the next one. The next document is part of the annex, 03615764 is the ERN number, and it's page 11 of the annex. It's on the ELMO. It is halfway down page 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So again we have the same story?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 11, after the paragraph, the short two-line -- barely two-line paragraph, the next page 03655763A, we need to insert another paragraph, next page, 03615764. Correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I believe you have understood quite clearly our situation. Can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow, Mr. Jones, or are you having problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, I can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, I would ask you to look at this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We have a technical problem. It shouldn't affect as such the proceedings, but it does affect the transmission of proceedings. It does affect the proceedings only insofar as -- if we try to put something on the ELMO, I think it will not reach us, or something like that. Yes, what's happening is that if a document is put on the ELMO, it does not show up on the monitor, so I can -- we can only proceed with the consent of both of you and of the accused, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also like to state that we're unable at this time period to put the document in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're happy to follow from hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the accused happy to follow too?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I did check with him briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. All right. So let's proceed. In the meantime, our men are doing what they can to try and fix the problem. Yes, sorry for the interruption, Ms. Sellers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, I would like you to look at this document and please tell the Trial Chamber your knowledge of the contents and the reason for the document.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also a report from the Srebrenica prosecutor submitted to the senior prosecutor in Tuzla upon her arrival in August 1995. She had, in the meantime, been assigned to the basic public prosecutor's office in Srebrenica, and that was why she drafted this report on the situation concerning the public prosecutor's office in Srebrenica at the time she was made to leave Srebrenica amid hostility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tankic, I would draw your attention to the paragraph in which she describes some of the conditions, the physical conditions, of the premises of the prosecutor's office, where it talks about the lack of some basic materials. Did this appear to be rather consistent through the different reports that were forwarded to your offices?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would also ask you to look further down that larger paragraph, and particularly where it begins to say: "Besides the task from its jurisdiction, the public prosecutor's office followed, by order of the Republic, the public prosecutor's office conducted the task of the high public prosecutor's office and the district military prosecutor's office, since the majority of perpetrators were from the RBiH army members." Has this also been something that is consistent within the reports that your office has received from the public prosecutor in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As we said yesterday, all of these reports are consistent with the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to pass on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We remain in the annex number 5, ERN number 03615758.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, once again, I would ask you to look at this document and please tell the Trial Chamber its origins or the reasons for its contents. Oh, I'm sorry, it's page 5 of the annex.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another report submitted to the high public prosecutor in Tuzla by the Srebrenica prosecutor while she was still with the basic public prosecutor's office in Tuzla. This report reflects the various types of crimes committed between the 1st of June, 1993, and July 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could please draw your attention to subheading 2, where a name of Ferid Mehmedovic appears. Within her capacity, would you acknowledge that it appears that the criminal situation described here was referred to the military district court in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This case was referred during the war to the district military court in Tuzla. However, the case was never pursued in 1995 and 1996. Therefore, the cantonal prosecutor, at least for as long as I was in the position, only completed this case as late as 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now ask you to look at subheading number 3, Sabit Begic. And is that the same situation where the Srebrenica prosecutor referred or handed the case over to the district military court in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please draw your attention to subheading 6, where we have Zuhirjet Omerovic, aka Beli. Is that a similar situation of the Srebrenica prosecutor referring or handing the case over to the district military court in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Certain investigative measures were taken later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would also draw your attention now, Mr. Tankic, to number 8, the case of Pasan Mujic and ask you once again, did the Srebrenica prosecutor refer or hand that case over to the district military court in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same applies as to the previous case. Certain investigative measures were taken. After that, the case was referred to the district military court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would now like to draw your attention to the paragraph that commences with "Aside from the above-named acts of murder, there were many criminal reports..." After number 9 and number 10, it appears to be the following paragraph. In that paragraph, it states: "In cases where criminal acts had been committed by members of the army of the Republic of BiH, we carried out certain investigative actions and handed the cases over to the county military court in Tuzla". Would that be a reflection of what occurred in the cases that we have just cited under number 2, 3, 6 and 8, paragraphs in this document?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is precisely what we talked about yesterday, and these eight cases were referred to the district military prosecutor in court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tankic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I would like to offer up a page of the dictionary, because I understand within the English version, sometimes we have the word "county" mentioned and at times we have the word "district" mentioned as it relates to district military court or county military court. And I would like to submit that this word seems to be slightly interchangeable within B/C/S. Might I hand up those to the Chamber, Defence counsel and to the witness. Your Honour, I understand that your pages are not highlighted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. I would ask you that, in the first column, if you would go to the bottom, there is a word there, it says "sud," that's how I would pronounce it, and then on the second column, if one would just go slightly below, halfway down, the word that says "okruzni".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Yes. And it says "okruzni: district court, county court, circuit court."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, Judge, do I take it -- because the Prosecution is submitting to us that in your country, in your language, for district court, county court and circuit court, you use the same word, which is "okruzni"; is that correct? Is that a correct submission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's give this a number. This will be 508.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we just have details as to what dictionary this is from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that. For the record now, Ms. Sellers, please, could you tell us where you got this from?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did receive it from a dictionary --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry, a dictionary which within our administrative support. I will have to give you the exact origin after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we would require is basically the front page, the first two or three pages, which show the details of the name of the dictionary, publisher, ISDN number, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. We will provide that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you will have them attached to this same page that we have just submitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. Your Honour, might I proceed, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. I would now like to have the witness look at the document ERN number 03648870.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, please look over the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we still in the annex or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I believe now that we are back in our new materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, I would ask you just to look at this document and could you confirm that this is a document that you handed the original to the office of the prosecutor during the proofing session.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and my signature confirms that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tankic, looking at this document, would you please tell the Trial Chamber its origin and its reason for having been created.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following her arrival from Srebrenica, the prosecutor reported orally on the situation in Srebrenica between 1993 and 1995, the high prosecutor then drew up this report and informed the relevant bodies, such as justice ministry of the republic of the BNH federation, the republic prosecutor and the justice minister of the Tuzla canton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, thank you. I would draw your attention to the last sentence in the first paragraph, which says the prosecutor's office was located in the building of the basic court in Srebrenica and beside the judge there was a typist and recording secretary, Beganovic Safet. Is that the municipal building that you testified about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1995, the prosecutor arrived in this building. Up until that point, the seat had been in the town hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the town hall what you referred to before as the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between June 1993 and 1995, the prosecutor reports that the prosecutor's office was in the municipal building or town hall and there was just one other department, the prosecution department, that was in the court premises, the court building where it used to be before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, does this document indicate, limited that it was, that there was some administrative assistance in the form of a typist and a recording secretary?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one person employed by the prosecutor who was a stenographer and a typist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I would now draw your attention to the last page of this document and in the English version it would be on page 4 of 4. And it starts after a listing of what appears to be types of crimes. I draw your attention to the sentence that states "an overall of 208 perpetrators have been reported out of which 110 were members of the BiH army, 41 criminal reports, 15 minor reports". Did that also appear consistent, that during the time period that the prosecutor in Srebrenica was in office, that a large percentage of reports concerned army members, members of the army?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only logical. Most able-bodied men were members of the army. It was only to be expected that this kind of complaint would be filed very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, lastly I just draw your attention to the last paragraph where the superior of the Srebrenica prosecutor is also confirming that cases pertaining to the army were handed over to the district military prosecutor's office in Tuzla. Is that in keeping with the responsibilities and duties of Ms. Helic to inform her superiors of that outcome?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means, there were always periodical reports on the state of affairs with the prosecutor's office, usually these would be annual reports and this would be one of these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to ask for a P number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered and received, marked as Prosecution Exhibit P509. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It's not really so much as an objection as just clarification that this will become apparent during the course of my cross-examination, there are sections missing from the English translation. It doesn't appear to be a complete version. So I'm wondering if I'm to understand there will be a complete English translation offered at some point and what one sees on page 2 of 4 skips text and there are other pages which haven't been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, certainly it's a very valid question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm happy that you brought that up. Since these documents were actually presented to the Office of the Prosecutor within the past two days, we endeavoured to have draft translations of what we thought were very important portions. Now that they have proper ERN numbers, they will be submitted for final translation and certainly those copies will then be distributed and substituted for the draft translations. Anything that appears to have been omitted or emphasized in a different manner, the Prosecution is certainly willing to address with Defence counsel. Our only intent was to try to facilitate that this witness could go forward with at least draft copies of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fair enough. Madam Registrar, please make note of this so that later on, when we come to examine the documents one by one, we will remember this and be able to check. Thank you. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, I believe you have document 03615757, which is part of the annex and it's page 3 of the annex. Would you please look at that. Mr. Tankic, I would ask you, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, now, parties and public ought to know that the communication with the ELMO has been reestablished, so you can actually look at the document on the ELMO, if you press the video evidence. Thank you. And I also thank the technicians for their quick and efficient response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, I would ask you to look at the first paragraph of that document, midway down -- oh, I'm sorry. I don't believe you answered my previous question when I asked you, Mr. Tankic, are you familiar with the document and what is the origin of this document. Could you please explain that to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an attachment or a complement to our earlier report. We see that the prosecutor remembered some further details and added this to her previous reports, especially as regards the identity of the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would draw your attention to midway down the first paragraph, a sentence that begins with "I would like to emphasize that not a single report to Srebrenica concerning both civilian and members of the army of the Republic of Bosnia remained unregistered or unprocessed. All reports were dealt with here." To your knowledge, would that mean that the reports that we have been discussing that came from the Srebrenica prosecutor's office were complete with any reports or crimes that had been alleged against members of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cases that were referred to the district military prosecutor were simply listed according to the names of suspects. All the remaining cases were cases against members of the army, initially filed with the Srebrenica prosecutor and eventually they remained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just now like to briefly go to the last document and that will conclude, Your Honours. That is a document found in the annex, page 1 of the annex, the ERN number is 03615756. Mr. Tankic, could you look at this document and please tell the Trial Chamber the origin or the reason for the existence of this document.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having received a report from the high public prosecutor in Srebrenica, the high prosecutor in Tuzla forwarded this to the justice ministry in Sarajevo, this information on the situation that prevailed and the cases that were underway in the military prosecutor's office in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, again, would this be in keeping with the proper procedure that Vildana Helic, your superior, was to follow in her role as senior public prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She was high prosecutor, and this would have been standard procedure for her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, my final question to you is that you have testified that people were obligated to report crimes that they knew of. Where does that obligation come from? What is the basis of such an obligation?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The provisions of the law on criminal procedure, adopted as a republican code.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers. Mr. Jones. Cross-examined by Mr. Jones:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge Tankic.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you agree that Srebrenica was physically, completely cut off from Tuzla from the start of the war until the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it right that Serb lines and minefields lay between Tuzla and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you are aware, wasn't it an extremely perilous journey to travel from Tuzla to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, if you're aware, even assuming that someone could make the journey from Tuzla, it would take several days, would it not, to get through all of the Serb lines, if travelling by foot.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware that many people lost their lives trying to travel by foot to and from Tuzla and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as far as communications between -- or communications with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Srebrenica are concerned, I think you've told us that the only way to communicate was by telegrams and by radio. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps some other ways, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what other ways?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you consider the case that we looked at where the civilian police filed a criminal complaint against a member of the army, both the suspect and the case itself arrived in Tuzla without actually using radio or telegrams. But I don't know what method was used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the case of Emir Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll return to that. Generally speaking, during the war in Tuzla, you knew very little of what was actually going on in Srebrenica; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your information in Tuzla was based mostly on what you got from the ham radio; would that be true?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were talking about the district military court which was in Tuzla during the war and which was established in September 1992. Now, firstly, that was a completely different entity from the Tuzla High Court, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for clarification, the Tuzla district military court would have been under the Ministry of Defence, whereas the High Court would be under the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The courts are supposed to be independent of ministries, either civilian or defence ministry, apart from certain administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the system of military justice, during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the military police and the military security service are connected to and work with the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the military security and its service is known by the acronym SVB, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the military prosecutor has jurisdiction to supervise and coordinate the activities of these organs, military police and SVB?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so it's part of the military prosecutor's job to issue requests to these organs to conduct investigations.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not conduct investigations, but some pretrial activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And conversely, it's the jurisdiction of the military prosecutor to receive reports about criminal acts committed by military personnel?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that includes reports about war crimes allegedly committed by military personnel. Sorry, I think your answer wasn't interpreted. Could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it -- isn't it right that, without a military prosecutor, in other words if that institution is not established, then it's not possible for the organs of the military police and the SVB to function legally.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could carry out certain duties, but they obviously could not carry out their duties as regards the prosecution. It wasn't their only task to file criminal charges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But as far as filing criminal charges is concerned, they would be operating in a vacuum, wouldn't they, if there wasn't a military prosecutor to direct them in their pretrial investigations; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that in the absence of a military prosecutor, the military police and the SVB can go about carrying out pretrial investigations and filing criminal reports, even though there's no military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could do it all apart from filing criminal reports, as far as there was no prosecutor, if I can explain that. They could secure the evidence, pieces of evidence. They could make reports on the crimes. And this was their duty, according to the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it would then stop there?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point, if there was no prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Well, I don't know if you can help us with this, but I put it to you that the military prosecutor for Srebrenica was not appointed until the 21st of May, 1995, less than two months before the fall of Srebrenica. Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military prosecutor in Tuzla had jurisdiction over the territory of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you've agreed, haven't you, that Tuzla was physically, completely separated from Srebrenica during that period.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from certain exceptions, which we saw yesterday and today as regards referral of certain cases and filing of certain charges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, I would like to pass up the first exhibit. It is a document of the district military prosecutor's office in Tuzla, and for the record it's number SU-4895A7795, and it's dated the 23rd of May, 1995. I would ask you, Judge Tankic, to have a close look at this document. Can you confirm that, according to this document, the RBH Assembly decided at its session on the 21st of May, 1995, to elect the three people whose names we see, Avdo Majstorovic, Dzemal Becirovic, and Ferid Otojagic, as "judges to the District Military Court in Tuzla, Srebrenica Department," and Resid Sinanovic was appointed at the same session to the post of deputy to the military district prosecutor in Tuzla, Srebrenica department. Do you agree that that's what's set out in that document?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In order to resolve the problems that we discussed here yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's right, isn't it, that before the 21st of May, 1995, there was no one physically in Srebrenica operating in the post of military judges or military prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was nobody else but civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would draw your attention to the following words in that document. It's page 1, third and fourth paragraphs. It says: "Please could you provide premises in Srebrenica for the military court department and military prosecutor's office, equipment, typewriters, office supplies, et cetera, and other requirements for their work. I hereby appoint Avdo Majstorovic, president of the military court, Srebrenica department, and he will create conditions suitable for the work of the department in cooperation with the mayor of the municipality and the commander of the division." Do you see that in the original? Have you seen that passage or those passages?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you agree as someone who has worked in the court system, that to coin a phrase, Rome wasn't built in a day, that even if this decision was dated the 23rd of May, 1995, it would actually take a considerable amount of time to find suitable personnel to equip a building and to get everything in order for the work to start?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also agree that it's all the more difficult if it's a town which is under siege, encircled by very hostile forces and facing genocide?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the characterisation. I understand what Defence counsel is trying to go to but I would ask that he rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's fair enough, Mr. Jones. I'm sure you understand too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure the witness has answered and I'm not sure what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has answered but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- what characterisation surely we're not disputing there was a genocide in July 1995 in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that that is in question in this case in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. So I'm not quite sure how I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Leave it. Let's move. He's answered the question in any case, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Point taken, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, isn't it right that the military court in Srebrenica hadn't even started functioning when Srebrenica fell to Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about the military court all the time, but here we are not talking about the military court but the department of the higher court in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to the department in Srebrenica, if I can put it that way, that department hadn't started properly functioning before Srebrenica fell to the Serbs. Is that something you're aware of or would agree with?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the time when this letter was sent, it is possible because only one and a half months later Srebrenica fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've seen from that document that the setting up of the court or the department was to be organized between the civilian and military authorities "in cooperation with mayor of the municipality and the commander of the division". You may be aware that the commander of the division, the 28th division, Naser Oric, had actually left the enclave of Srebrenica in early April 1995, to go to Tuzla. Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the time when he left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I would ask simply to have an exhibit number for this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We need the sequence, Madam Registrar, please. What number shall we give this document? Next number for the Defence document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 205, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D205. So this document -- this did not have an ERN, did it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think I better give some details -- this document tendered by the Defence being a letter from the president of the military court and district military prosecutor in Tuzla, dated 25th of May, addressed to the chief of Srebrenica municipality, commander of the 28th division, Srebrenica, as being tendered, received and marked as Defence Exhibit D205.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Judge Tankic, it's true, isn't it, that during the war, the law on regular courts applied on the territory of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the law on criminal proceedings of the RBH also applied during the war? Sorry, of the SFRY was adopted for the RBH?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these laws regulated, didn't they, the territorial and subject-matter jurisdiction of the courts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Criminal procedure acts did not regulate subject-matter jurisdiction, but there was a special offer that, whereas territorial jurisdiction is indeed regulated by the Criminal Procedure Act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And isn't it right that according to the law on regular courts, only the highest state organs of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina could establish -- had jurisdiction to establish a military court or military department, military court department?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only -- so the prosecutor's office or a court could have been established only by law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But isn't it true that it could only be established by the republican bodies in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of the war, it was only up to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And we saw that I think in Prosecution Exhibit P497 which we saw yesterday, it was the statutory order on district military courts and that was signed by the president of the Presidency. We have another exhibit on this subject, with the Usher's assistance, it's a decision on appointing judges to district military courts and just for the record it's decision number 02111900/92, dated 21 December, 1992, published in the official gazette number 24, page 640 on 28th of December, 1992. And it's item 575, firstly. There we see appointments to the Tuzla, Zenica and Travnik district military courts. Do you see that? And that's a decision signed by the president of the Presidency. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the same page we have number 574, that's the appointment of military prosecutors and, again, that's an act for which the RBH Presidency is the authorised body, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when we consider the situation of Srebrenica in the establishment of a department of Tuzla district military courts, only the RBH Presidency had authority to do that, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. In the previous document, whereby the department was established, I'm not sure about that. But I'm sure about the court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You're sure that --

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And about the prosecution office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So only the RBH Presidency had the jurisdiction to establish district military court and district military prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's told you as regards the court, establishment of a court, yes. As regards the establishment of a prosecutor, he is not sure. That's how I read his words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Well, what I understand is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I stand to be corrected of course because it wouldn't be the first time I have misunderstood something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Presidency appointed judges and prosecutors, but I'm not sure whose jurisdiction it was to establish court departments. That should have been written in the previous document we saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I'll come back to that in a moment. For the meantime I would ask for an exhibit number for that page of the official gazette. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will -- first of all, it has ERN number 01194983 as being tendered by the Defence and admitted as such and marked as Defence Exhibit D206.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So would you agree, Judge Tankic, that the authorities in Srebrenica, for example, the Srebrenica War Presidency, if that's a body which you're familiar with, had no authority on their own to elect or appoint military judges or military prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I heard him say "no". But I see "yes" on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Could you clarify please Judge Tankic whether --

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not authorised to establish courts. Or if there was, the War Presidency in Srebrenica, they were not authorised to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So it follows from that doesn't it, that if they purported to establish such a court, they would have no legal authority?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also, according to the law, if a military commander -- or a military commander would not have any authority to elect or appoint judges and prosecutors to military court, would it?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, apart from special military courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Special military courts are established to deal with breaches of discipline, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't there jurisdiction crimes against the ABiH, taking the case of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, crimes against the army insubordination, treason, desertion, those sorts of offences?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For these criminal offences, for these disciplinary breaches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A different jurisdiction from the jurisdiction of the Tuzla district military court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could try similar criminal offences, but under specific circumstances prescribed by the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Namely, if those offences constitute disciplinary breaches?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but if they have features of criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll return to that and look at the actual provisions in due course. But sticking with district military courts and departments of those courts, do you agree it would be wrong for a commander to abrogate to himself the power to appoint judges and prosecutors to those courts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which courts, the special courts?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. The district military court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: District military courts, okay.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm moving on to another exhibit, and so perhaps this is a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Just to say, I am hoping to finish today, but I've had 48 minutes so far, and I've probably got two hours or so. As I say, I hope we can finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will try and do our best. What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a moment. This is jinxed. The moment Mr. Jones said he'll do his best to finish today, we have a technical problem. If what you need to say needs to go on the record, there is no point in me asking you to proceed, Ms. Sellers, because all it says, it's reminding me when we took the recess, at what time. What I'd like to know is how much we have to wait, roughly, so that, if we need to stay in the courtroom, we'll stay in the courtroom. If it's going to take longer, obviously each one goes to his own room, including the witness, because ... What they are doing is they are creating a new -- they are dividing the session into two parts. I see a "test", we are having "test", so I presume that we are in a position to proceed? I thank whoever is responsible for having solved this problem. I see that now the transcript of the sitting is divided into two files. This is the second file. Okay, let's proceed. Mr. Jones, I would appreciate it if you would try to do your level best to finish today. Yes, Ms. Somers -- Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting counsel. I just want to say, in the request of the Chamber to have the cover pages of the dictionary and the other pages, that we have been able to provide that for you now and I would like to hand it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would just remind you that this has already been marked Prosecution Exhibit 508, and one would have to attach the pages of the dictionary that were previously handed up to these four pages here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Sellers. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I will go as quickly as I can, and perhaps we can even have a shorter second break. I don't know, with the agreement of the technicians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will try to do our best.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. May I also -- I presume there will be one clean transcript for the day and not two, just a matter which -- we've now got two transcripts, as you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but that is technically the easiest thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, they will then convert it, bring them together --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and we will have one transcript. But for the purpose of the record, I had to state that we have a new, sort of, transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Judge Tankic, I'm going to ask you some questions about the special military courts which we were discussing before the break, but if I can preface those questions by asking you the following: When you were shown the chart, this chart yesterday, you may recall, you said: "I have very little knowledge about military structures and military issues." It's correct, isn't it, that you, in fact, never served as a military judge?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so your experience of military structures, military issues, is based on your experience of compulsory service in the JNA; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as well as the reserve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. It's not based on any experience which you had serving in the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you complete your compulsory military service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I would ask if the witness could be shown Prosecution Exhibit P323, which is the Decree Law on Special Military Courts. And the ERN -- I don't know if it's necessary to read it, really, for the record, but it's 00630020. And our apologies. This wasn't on our list. It only arose in light of answers which this witness gave this morning, or information which he volunteered this morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge Tankic, I would ask you to look at Article 3 of this decree law. It's on the first page in the -- both in English and B/C/S. Isn't it right that Article 3 sets out the jurisdiction of the court, and it says: "The Court shall try service men for criminal forces committed against the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Article 3, which you see down in the bottom on the right-hand column.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we see the list of crimes, and just to generally characterize them, without going through all of them, would you agree that they're crimes such as failure to comply with an order, opposing orders of a superior, offences such as mutiny, treason, desertion; in other words, all offences against army discipline. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the jurisdiction of these special military courts is crimes against the armed forces of the republic, the special military court would not have jurisdiction, would it, to try someone for crimes committed against the enemy?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I've finished with that exhibit. Now, I'm going back to the Tuzla district military court, and we have a new exhibit, which is a document from the -- from the Tuzla district military court, and it's SU-4895, dated 24 April 1995. And it's a suggestion of the appointment of judges and prosecutors in the department of the military court in Srebrenica. If you could take a moment, Judge Tankic, to read that document. And, in particular, I draw your attention to two sentences on page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S, and it's the sentence towards the end of the paragraph which says: "This court, i.e., the Tuzla district military court, is not able to make any decisions before it receives a request for conduct of an investigation or an indictment from the military prosecutor. Therefore, according to the law, it is not able to cover detentions before receiving the criminal charges, i.e., a request for conduct of an investigation." Now, do you agree with that, that is a correct statement of the law?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in other words, the Tuzla district military court could not authorise the detention of a suspect for any significant period of time unless and until criminal charges were submitted by the military prosecutor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And without a military prosecutor in Srebrenica, those charges could not be physically submitted by authorities in Srebrenica; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, they could not be --

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, they couldn't, but it -- in a certain way they could, which you can clearly see if you look at the data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Well, we'll come to that. Dealing with the military prosecutor in Tuzla, would you agree that they weren't in a position to conduct investigations on the ground in Srebrenica because of the physical separation?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just a small correction. An investigating magistrate or judge and not the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So is it right that the detention in Srebrenica of persons suspected -- of military personnel suspected of serious crimes under the jurisdiction of the Tuzla district military court, could not, in practical terms, be authorised until at least the 24th of April, 1995, the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand this, but I'll try to answer. I believe I'll get the context right. The suspect could be detained pursuant to a request by a civilian prosecutor. However, detention could only be extended with the Tuzla military courts, which is precisely what was done in the nine cases that we looked at. If a serious crime has been committed or if the perpetrator was a dangerous person, they had to find a way to isolate this individual from the environment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And if there wasn't -- until there was an extension by the Tuzla military court, how long could a person be held on the authority of the civilian prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the law in wartime circumstances, 15 days. Even the police forces were authorised to detain any person for up to three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, if authorization for continued detention was not received, the person would have to be released under the law; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Released from detention, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd ask for this document to be given an exhibit number as well, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document will become D207.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a few questions about the civilian courts and about the jurisdiction of the Tuzla higher court. Now, before the 1st of June 1993, not even a lower court existed in Srebrenica, did it?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, does that mean no lower court did exist prior to the 1st of June 1993, or it didn't?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't prior to the 1st of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And taking the 1st of June 1993, that is, isn't it, after the demilitarisation of the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You're aware that Srebrenica was declared a safe area and that United Nations was then charged with demilitarising the enclave?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I put it to you that that was in April 1993, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at that point, 1st of June, 1993, with the enclave being demilitarised, isn't it right that the military police stopped functioning and lost jurisdiction to act within the enclave, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was going on in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as a matter of law and as a matter of logic, wouldn't it follow that you can't have a military police in a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness doesn't know the answer to the question, I think even this rephrasing doesn't assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Ms. Sellers has a point here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could the witness be shown P506, Prosecution Exhibit P506. It's the second page is the actual report rather than the cover note and it's 03648882. I draw your attention to the first sentence which I think we've seen already "during 1994, the Srebrenica public prosecutor's office received 144 criminal reports from the public security station and two reports from physical entities". Now, the public security station is the civilian police station, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So isn't it correct that from the very start of her work, Ms. Akagic was receiving reports only from the civilian police. She didn't receive any from the military police?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report would seem to indicate that she did not receive any from the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I put it to you and it may be something that you can help with, or maybe not, but that's because the military police was no longer functioning after demilitarisation. I've made that point already and I... The witness may answer if he chooses to, otherwise I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you proceed with your next question because that is a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry. If the witness could now be shown P501. This document refers to the start -- starting of the work of the prosecutor on the 1st of June 1993, and I draw your attention to the third paragraph in the English, in any event, in English it says: "It needs to be pointed out that the procedure ends once the indictment is issued because of the general situation the court conducts, just and investigation. The process of conducting the investigation is being burdened by the lack of experts from many fields who could give their opinion". On the other hand payment system is nonexistent, in other words the value of the stolen goods cannot be expressed in terms of money and therefore correct classification of the crimes cannot be carried out." Now based on that my question is: Do you agree from that that the lower court in Srebrenica could only barely carry out an investigation and that it was impossible to carry out a full investigation because of the general situation, i.e., being under siege and under constant attack?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the reasons, but the prosecutor's report indicates how far criminal proceedings usually got, although people were tried for minor crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just as far as your knowledge of the situation in Srebrenica was concerned, did you ever go to Srebrenica during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, isn't it right that Ms. Akagic opened investigations into serious crimes only when it was as I believe the phrase is in your law and language "dangerous to postpone", in other words, where due to the urgency of the situation, evidence might be lost, if there were not an immediate investigation?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And doesn't your law provide that in that situation, even an unauthorized person can conduct an investigation into serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only persons actually authorised by law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Ms. Akagic was not authorised or did not have jurisdiction over serious crimes, did she, because she was the prosecutor of the lower court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she didn't, but in urgent situations she had authority to give relevant orders to the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could be shown P506. And it's the last paragraph of that exhibit. And stated there: "I would like to point out that the Srebrenica basic court does not act according to the indictment proposals, the first instance public prosecutor's office, accept in some cases of forest theft and illegal seizures of state-owned immoveable property. The basic court is only opening investigations and undertaking certain investigative measures following a request of this prosecutor's office". My question is, isn't it apparent from that that the basic court in Srebrenica was basically not -- not functioning or at least functioning only in the most minimal way during this period?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report indicates that in part it was functioning up to the point of trial, with the exception of minor crimes, as we said before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. In other words, it was impossible to actually hold trials in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were shown earlier today P505 and I won't ask in the interests of time -- I won't ask that to be actually be put before you, but you'll recall that there was reference to the premises where the prosecutor's office was located and that refugees had destroyed all the documentation of the public prosecutor's office. Two questions about that.
