Firstly, would you agree as someone who spent much of his life working in the court system, that the destruction of documentation of the public prosecutor's office would gravely impede the work of a prosecutor trying to get started, in other words, if regulations and decrees, et cetera, had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question. If you have a specific case, that would take some reconstructing and it would obviously prove very difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, well, let's take a different angle. You said that you assumed that among the destroyed documents there were not cases which had arisen during the war because you said you assumed that refugees had been in that building from the start of the war. Now in fact that is quite an assumption, isn't it, that's not something which you have any knowledge of whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if that's wrong, if refugees, let's say, only arrived in March 1993, it's possible that they would have destroyed case files from February, January 1993 and from 1992. Do you accept that that is possible?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who, destroyed by whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Refugees who were in that building, the fact is you don't know what they destroyed, do you? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the prosecutor's report indicates that she, in fact, assumes that those had been destroyed by the refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well it's not stated there as an assumption, but we can move on from that. Now, according to the law on criminal proceedings of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, only higher courts could try the most serious crimes, including murder and war crimes. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a lower court could not unilaterally decide to give itself jurisdiction over serious crimes, could it?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would require a decision of the authorised state organ to empower the lower court to be able to try those crimes, correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact in Srebrenica, there never existed a higher court with jurisdiction over those crimes, did there, it was merely a transfer of jurisdiction at a certain point?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could briefly look at P503 again, and that's the document from the higher public prosecutor in Tuzla, dated 5th of January 1994. You saw this yesterday, it's two documents, Tuzla to Sarajevo and Tuzla to Srebrenica. And the date of the first document is the 5th of January 1994. It's clear from that, isn't it, that the public prosecutor's office in Srebrenica requested a transfer of jurisdiction so that it could handle cases which came under the authority of the Tuzla higher court.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that request was taken up by the Tuzla prosecutor's office requesting a decision from the Ministry of Justice and administration in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was for the Ministry of Justice in Sarajevo to take that decision?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we saw, from that document, that the reasons for the request is the physical detachment between Srebrenica and Tuzla. And isn't it right --

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And the prosecutor and president of the Tuzla High Court, who were addressing this letter to the authorities in Sarajevo, explained that it's necessary and urgent because murders and aggravated thefts and other crimes had been carried out in the Srebrenica area. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So isn't it fair to summarise that, from this letter that the lower court and prosecutor in Srebrenica couldn't do anything that deal with misdemeanours unless and until the authorised state institution gave permission for the transfer of jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. The law of criminal procedure provides that they can in fact take certain preinvestigative measures or order detention in urgent cases, but they must, at the same time, inform the relevant prosecutors and the relevant court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Now, we have another exhibit which is a document from the public prosecutor's office in Tuzla dated 1st of March 1994. This may already be part of P505?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry about it. If it is, let's proceed, Mr. Jones. I think let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We found it easier -- with the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take the practical approach and -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is simply to ask you to confirm this, Judge Tankic, that it wasn't in fact until the 1st of March 1994 that the transfer of jurisdiction from the Tuzla higher court to Srebrenica was communicated to the authorities in Srebrenica or to the prosecutor in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the day when it was communicated, but the decision was taken in January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And even then, that court, the lower court with this expanded jurisdiction, did not have jurisdiction over military personnel in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It had no jurisdiction over them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would ask for that document to be given an exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That document is being given number, Defence Exhibit D208.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you didn't in fact go to Srebrenica during the war. It follows from that, doesn't it -- or if you could tell us, you don't know to what extent the public security station in Srebrenica was functional during the war?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the criminal charges were filed to the prosecutor by that station, so it only follows that it was operational.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the extent to which it was operational is something which is outside your knowledge, isn't it, the extent to which it had investigators or technicians to carry out forensic investigations?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you and you may or may not be able to help with this, but that most of the trained and professional people fled Srebrenica at the start of the war and that there were, therefore, very few trained professional policemen and investigators in Srebrenica during the war.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the basic prosecutor was the only one with bar examination out of all the lawyers there. Judges had no bar examination, although they did graduate from the law school. I'm not aware of the police structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear stories in Tuzla of professional people and educated people having left Srebrenica at the start of the war?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't true only of Srebrenica, but of the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would also suggest and again only if you can help us with this, but that the relevant equipment for carrying out investigations, cameras, audiotapes, et cetera, were not available in Srebrenica. Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the reports coming out from the public security centre and from criminal charges that were pressed, we can see that they did attach some drawings and some photo documentation, so I could not entirely agree with your statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sticking with that drawings, et cetera, those couldn't be sent to Tuzla by radio, could they? Or even by telegram?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were objective reasons which prevented the cases mentioned by the prosecutor to be submitted to the military prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So in other words, when you said "yes", you meant they could not be sent to Tuzla drawings and that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It could not communicate by telegrams.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Telegram was just for text messages, correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to explore a hypothetical about referring a case to Tuzla with you for a moment. And I want you to put yourself in the position of the Tuzla district military prosecutor. Now, if you were informed by radio that unknown thousands of civilians had stolen Serb property and caused damage to Serb property, would you consider that a serious criminal referral? Or would you consider it perhaps even vexatious, in other words, a waste of your time and resources to receive a complaint of that nature?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, I would just ask that Defence counsel, in formulating this hypothetical, does he clearly mean that the thousands of civilians are under the jurisdiction of the district military court in Tuzla, or is he proffering a hypothetical that is not necessarily in line with the law that we have had testimony about so far?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that is a fair question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. My understanding -- well, I take the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's remove the referral to the military court, any sort of a referral. If you were a prosecutor, civilian or military, and you received complaints saying that, in Srebrenica, thousands of civilians had committed -- unknown civilians had committed crimes against property, would that be a proper complaint?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a report on the basis of which a prosecutor can commence his work and can address law and order agencies, in view of checking out these allegations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday how complaints would be sent back if they were incomplete. Surely, this would be the sort of complaint which would be sent back as incomplete?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I did not say that complaints were sent back but that they were checked via various organs, such as the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree that certain means and professional people are necessary for the most basic and simple investigations?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that, in April 1992, when the Serbs occupied Srebrenica, that they took away from the police station, from the public security station, all the equipment necessary for police work? Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also agree that, in order to conduct any kind of proper investigation, apart from people and equipment, it's also necessary to have regulations so that those carrying out the investigations do so in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, if we could pass up the next exhibit. It's a document from the primary court in Srebrenica, dated 10th of December, 1993, number SU-293, and it's information on the operation of the Srebrenica lower court. In fact, it has an ERN 01840660 to 01840661.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to, first of all, draw your attention to the first paragraph: "At the beginning of the war, in April 1992, the Lower Court Public Prosecutor's Office, Misdemeanours Court, and all government organs in Srebrenica ceased to operate". Now, are you aware that when the war started all the judicial and political organs in Srebrenica ceased to operate?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly cannot say that I had no knowledge on the situation in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at the part of the second paragraph discussing the so-called misdemeanours court in Srebrenica. It says: "Due to the chaotic situation, isolation of the republic, lack of legal regulatory framework, and other reasons, the work of the Misdemeanours Court was symbolic". And then the document discusses the attempts made to deal with the chaotic situation, including the War Presidency issuing a decision that the public security station would carry out investigations, but only with a maximum of six months' imprisonment. My question is: A maximum of six months' imprisonment was the maximum sentence for misdemeanours under the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The misdemeanour court could also sentence somebody to imprisonment. In peacetime, it was the imprisonment of up to two months. I'm not sure whether the same applied in war circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I would direct your attention to the bottom paragraph on page 2. In the original, it's the fourth paragraph from the bottom on page 2, starting with the third sentence: "We are not able to conduct appropriate expert analyses due to the shortage of relevant experts on the territory under this court's jurisdiction. Also, we are not able to provide defence counsels for perpetrators of crimes which require mandatory defence." And then further down, the last sentence in the same paragraph: "We received Official Gazettes for 1992 and 1993 only in November 1993 and they are incomplete." The Official Gazette sets out all the decrees, laws and regulations that have been adopted for the functioning of organs in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware that the Official Gazette was only received, or the Official Gazettes were only received in Srebrenica in November 1993 and then only in incomplete form?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when they received them, but I do know that the court was established on the 1st of June and it had to be established in accordance with the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, I would draw your attention to the last three paragraphs of this document: "Currently, we have problems due to the shortage of appropriate forms and typing paper. Refugees are accommodated in the lower court building and the court archives have been totally destroyed. We are doing the best in the circumstances to protect the rule of law. We would appreciate it if you could send us instructions with regard to extension of detention for criminal offenders and other relevant instructions in light of the specific situation we're experiencing." You are aware, aren't you, that, in general, there were these severe problems in maintaining a judicial system in Srebrenica at this time?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask for an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this document is being tendered and admitted and recorded as Defence Exhibit D209.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D209, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And with the usher's assistance, we have another exhibit, which is from the command of the 8th Operational Group, Srebrenica, dated the 10th of September, 1994; number 1301476 of 94. The ERN is 01838620.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we spoke earlier about special military courts, which we see referred to in the first paragraph of that document. Now, reading the first paragraph of that document, from September 1994, isn't it clear that, in fact, the decree law on special military courts had not even been received by the security organs of the armed forces in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what issues from these -- from this letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would ask you to look at the third paragraph as well: "We are requesting information on the responsible institution in cases where a soldier commits an offence outside of his military duty (whether he would be prosecuted for disciplinary liability or would a civilian court be responsible)." And I would ask: Isn't it plain, from this, that in Srebrenica, even in September 1994, the military didn't know who had jurisdiction and authority to conduct proceedings against members of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot conclude that from this paragraph. This is only the legal question on whether a civilian court has jurisdiction over a person who is not a military person or whether a disciplinary court has jurisdiction over that. You might conclude that, but...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The assistant commander for security, Nedzad Bektic, certainly appears, from this, to be confused about who would have jurisdiction in this case, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask for an exhibit number for this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be document -- Defence document D210.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies to the usher for the constant exhibits but we're nearly through. There is another exhibit which is a document from the primary court in Srebrenica, number SU-594, dated 14 February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is an urgent communication -- I will ask you to confirm; -- from the president of the Srebrenica lower court, Mr. Mensud Omerovic to the military of justice and administration in Sarajevo. And it refers, does it not, to an earlier memorandum which was sent "detailing several practical problems we've encountered due to the war, the fact that Srebrenica is surrounded and the impossibility of acting in accordance with certain provisions of the ZKP law on criminal procedure". I would ask you also, before I ask you a question about this document, to look at the last sentence of the second paragraph: "The court is unable to appoint defence counsel to defend the accused ex officio because there is not a single attorney in Srebrenica and none of the lawyers here wishes to accept his - that's referring to Nasif Mesanovic, his defence." My question is, would you agree that suspected perpetrators of the most serious crimes still have the right to counsel and a fair trial?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The court president was obviously not aware of the law, because at this time the defence counsel could be any person, not even a lawyer, any person who could assist a suspect during the criminal procedures. This letter was written before that first information from March about the jurisdiction of the higher court and higher prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you consider that would be a safe procedure for guaranteeing a fair trial, to have a nonlawyer person appointed to represent an accused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well I think I can dispense the witness from answering that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think let's move to something else, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I would ask for an exhibit number for that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be D211.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now possibly a final exhibit or one of the last ones. This is a special report which we're handing up now, from the intelligence division, army headquarters, dated 13 July 1995 to the chairman of the Presidency of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The ERN is 01854496 to 01854497. My question first is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why 4497 and not 4499?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Will you bear with me for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see that the English translation stops basically at 4497.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The B/C/S one goes to 4499. If you have no intention of tendering also the last two pages, we can remove them. If you want to keep them there, we keep them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It should be the whole lot. Right to 01854499. Thank you, Your Honour, for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, firstly, isn't it correct, if you know, that telegraphic and helicopter connections with Tuzla were established only after the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, i.e., after April 1993? First, if you know that.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know at what time it occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well turning to this document which is dated 13th of July, 1995, firstly, that's clearly written, isn't it, in the midst of the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the passage dealing with helicopter flight to Srebrenica and Zepa, it says: There were 17 helicopter overflights and each time a helicopter was shot." Now it would be wrong to suggest, wouldn't it, that there was a regular service by helicopter between Srebrenica and Tuzla at any time between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree, if this is within your competence, that if a helicopter did get shot down over Serb territory, the Serbs could have of course help themselves to whatever documents they found and used them for propaganda purposes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this is speculation. I mean it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How would the witness know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just from living through the war and being in Tuzla, but very well, Your Honour. I would simply ask for a Defence exhibit number for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be Defence Exhibit D212.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've seen cases or at least a case of murder which was referred by the Srebrenica prosecutor to the court in Tuzla. The next document - my apologies, with the usher's assistance - is issued by the 8th operational group Srebrenica. It's number 130524, dated 23rd of February 1995. Annexed to the document is an official letter from the lower court in Srebrenica number SU-1395. If you could just take the time to look at that document briefly. Now, can you confirm -- and as I say, take your time -- but that the letter from the lower court is expressing concerns about detaining military personnel while awaiting detention orders from the military district court in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And among other complaints, isn't the president of the Srebrenica lower court Mensud Omerovic saying that as a result of the delays in receiving authorization from Tuzla to detain suspects "in consequence, even some responsible individuals believe that the work of the lower court is unlawful". Have you found that passage in the original? Sorry, you have to give a verbal answer, if you see it.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right isn't it that even a court cannot detain people beyond the period prescribed by law and that under Bosnian law, if it does so, the court itself is acting unlawfully?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have under Bosnian law a crime of false imprisonment? In other words, I can rephrase it?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it exists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if you look at the second to last paragraph, you see the following: "As it has been almost three months since our court ordered detention and the district military court has not sent detention orders or orders to end detention to the accused persons, there have been beliefs that the court has been acting unlawfully in exercising laws of its own." My question is, it was, at this time, it was still only the Tuzla district military court which could authorise detention for members of the ABiH suspected of committing serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you aware, when you were in Tuzla, that there were delays of this nature of up to three months during which the Srebrenica lower court awaited a response from the Tuzla district military court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And isn't it also clear from this letter that the president of the Srebrenica lower court was so frustrated that he told Tuzla that they would no longer deal with cases under the jurisdiction of the Tuzla district military court, because "this court, due to the lack of support, shall no longer deal with cases which were under the jurisdiction of the district military court, that is, cases against members of the ABiH army regardless of the type of crime they committed and particularly that this court will not order detention in any of the cases. We are informing you of this so that you can take the necessary steps to assume responsibility in the free area of the municipality of Srebrenica." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the courts acted under the law and everything that he states here is in perfect compliance with the legal regulations, or rather, the specific position that he expresses here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact isn't he essentially throwing up his arms and saying that his court will no longer deal with these sorts of cases because of the impossibility of ordering detention of these long periods?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military district court in Tuzla has sole jurisdiction of the military persons, so what he concludes here is only too logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't it also show, this letter, that in fact the jurisdiction of the Tuzla district military court over crimes in Srebrenica was almost purely theoretical. It wasn't a real effective jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult to exercise that jurisdiction, that much is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask for an exhibit number for that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be 213, D213.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. We have another document now, which is from the Tuzla district military court, SU-4895, or 48/95, dated 14th April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you take a moment to read this letter briefly, it's a response, is it not, from the president of the military court in Tuzla to the repeated requests from the president of the Srebrenica lower court to solve some of the problems that we saw. If you could pay attention to the following passage: "It is clear that the matter of solving cases that concern persons in Srebrenica and that come under the jurisdiction of the district military court cannot be resolved satisfactorily despite the efforts by the lower court in Srebrenica and the district military court in Tuzla." So would you agree that this document speaks of an impasse in administering military justice in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the delays of the decisions on detention, line 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. That problem has reached crisis point. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All problems had reached crisis point already, any way you look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is April 1995 so, would you agree, three months before the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we see the solution proposed by the president of the military court in Tuzla: "Therefore, the president of this court has written several times insisting and demanding that the military court department be set up in Srebrenica in accordance with the decision issued by the RBH Presidency. Unfortunately, we still haven't received nominations for the appointment of at least two judges to the military court in Tuzla, Srebrenica department. This is apparently the case because they do not have any graduate lawyers."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can counsel please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. I wonder if the booth has copies of the exhibits, if it's possible to enquire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't ask me. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I will go slower nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It very much depends on whether you provide them with a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we did. It was just to check. I'll go more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, can you confirm that the letter goes on to enquire whether certain graduate lawyers are still living in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in order to set up a proposal to appoint judges in that department of the military court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this proposal to set up a military court department, that, again, is something I think you've confirmed already, but which could only be adopted by the competent republican state organ; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Presidency of the republic. In fact, the Presidency did pass a decision to set that up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And isn't it right that that's why the president of the Tuzla court is requesting the president of the Srebrenica court to provide information about graduate lawyers so that Tuzla can propose the nomination of those persons by the authorities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's for the Sarajevo authorities to actually appoint them?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if we can have an exhibit number for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be D214.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you some questions about the Emir Halilovic case, which has been discussed already. And for the record, and if it assists, Defence Exhibit D119, War Hospital, refers to that at page 113. I just say that in case that may be of any assistance. We have another exhibit from the district military court in Tuzla, number KI-600/93, dated 20 August 1993. Sorry, forgive me a moment. This is another document on the same case, and it's a decision to conduct an investigation into Emir Halilovic on the basis of suspicion of committing three murders, Slobodan Zekic, Zagorka Zekic, Stojan Krsmanovic. And the decision is signed by an investigative judge of the military district court in Tuzla. I simply want to ask you this about the case of Emir Halilovic. Isn't -- on the distinctive features of that case, that, firstly, he was caught red-handed after the third murder; in other words, he was arrested immediately after he committed the third of the three murders. And secondly, that UNPROFOR cooperated in airlifting Halilovic by helicopter to Tuzla. Would you agree that those are two features of the Emir Halilovic case?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how he was taken to Tuzla. I simply don't know. I know that he arrived in Tuzla along with the respective criminal complaint, or rather, charges and that was also where he was prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware --

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that was only following the third murder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware, from having spent the war in Tuzla, perhaps having seen convoys of people arriving from Srebrenica, that people were desperate to leave the enclave?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, from having been in Tuzla during the war, that people from Srebrenica were desperate to leave the enclave and were arriving in Tuzla, crammed into lorries whenever they could?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you agree that it was very rare for UNPROFOR to airlift a Bosniak out of Srebrenica by helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, if he has knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Extremely exceptional.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It calls for a bit of speculation on his part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He may have knowledge about this. I wouldn't exclude knowledge on the part of the witness of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He has answered in the meantime. Could I have an exhibit number for that last exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be D215 [Realtime transcript read in error "D"].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could be shown P507, please, which also deals with Emir Halilovic. This is dated the 28th of July, 1993. In fact -- in fact, my apologies, it's not in fact necessary to show the witness the exhibit. I can ask questions without the aid of the exhibit. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, because I notice that on page 32, line 1, the exhibit number does not show up in the transcript. I said that will be D215. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It was just to ask this, Judge Tankic, about Emir Halilovic. It's correct, isn't it, that he was indeed brought to justice in Tuzla for killing three persons of Serbian nationality?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that, following his conviction, he was subjected to psychiatric assessment and found to have a brain tumour and died shortly after that had been diagnosed?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've also been asked about the case of Pasan Mujic, who attempted to kill his wife and who did kill his mother-in-law. Would you agree that it was possible to deal with him in Tuzla because he had actually reached the free territory of Tuzla after the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995; in other words, that that's why the case was able to progress to the trial stage?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I have some questions now about the court archives in Srebrenica and the fall of Srebrenica. If you could be shown P505. And in the B/C/S it's ERN 03615758; in the English, it should be page 5 of 22. I say "should be" because it hasn't always been easy to navigate. This is a document from Dzuzida Akagic, dated, I think it is, the 3rd of November, 1995, so four months after the fall of Srebrenica. And it states: "Having in mind the unexpected development of the situation in Srebrenica, which is known to everyone, all cases of the basic public office of the prosecutor were left in the building of the basic court in Srebrenica on the second floor." I don't know if you see that. The page is 03615758, at the top right-hand corner. It should be [B/C/S spoken], in the third paragraph, second sentence. Do you agree, firstly, that that phrase, "the unexpected development of the situation in Srebrenica," refers to the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you understand, from this, or did you understand when you read this document, that as a result of the sudden, unexpected fall of Srebrenica, the prosecutor and judges had to flee and that they left all the court files behind?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't exclude the possibility, do you, when you say that -- well, you don't exclude the possibility, do you, that there were cases in Srebrenica which were never pursued or transferred to Tuzla precisely because of the fall of Srebrenica and the loss of the archives?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't exclude that possibility, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I refer you to 03615764 of the same exhibit, and in English, it should be page 10 of 22. It's halfway down the page in the B/C/S, where it says [B/C/S spoken]. It has the date 7/7/93, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In English?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It should be page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in English, it's: "The public prosecutor's office, Srebrenica, was working until 7/7/1995 when an offence on Srebrenica started and when we had to leave Srebrenica as displaced persons on 13/7/1995. As a result of an unexpected situation, the following documentation of the public prosecutor's office had remained in Srebrenica." Do you see that, Judge Tankic?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it says to round and one square seals, and then, "about 33 case files from 1993." According to that, then, isn't it correct that 33 case files dating from 1993 remained in Srebrenica when it fell to the Serbs? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know, do you, whether those concerned serious crimes within the jurisdiction of the higher court or less serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, based on the report, about the types of crimes committed in 1993, because the crimes, the actual crimes, we're enumerated, most of them being minor crimes and not serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to pursue that with you a little. You said that war crimes cases weren't referred to Tuzla. But isn't it correct that some of the murders which were referred - and I will take the example of Emir Halilovic, which involved -- one of the murders involved killing a Serb who was in the hospital in Srebrenica - could have been qualified as war crimes, arguably, but may have simply been characterized as ordinary crimes by the prosecutor. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think I can allow that question, Mr. Jones. That's not for the witness to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So be it, Your Honour. I would ask the witness to be shown Exhibit P501, though, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can look at that exhibit and the lines which are numbered 2 and 3. I'm hoping you can help us with this. I'll wait until you have it in front of you. Lines 2 and 3 refer to Articles 147 and 148 of the RBiH Criminal Code; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if the RBiH code is the same as the SFRY code, Article 147 is in fact marauding, Article 148 is making use of forbidden means of warfare, this is according to P496, which are in the section criminal acts against humanity and international law. So I wonder if you can help us with an explanation of why you say that none of the crimes which were referred were actually war crimes.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply because all these are crimes described in the Criminal Code of the republic of BNH, but these crimes are not provided for there, but rather in the special provisions of the Criminal Code of the SFRY, which was then adopted as a republican law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So under republican law, which articles referred to war crimes?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that war crimes were not criminalised under republican law?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in the Criminal Code that was adopted from the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Well, I won't pursue that. Now you were asked a number of questions yesterday about Dzuzida Akagic and her competence and professionalism and how she dealt with the situation in Srebrenica. So I take it you consider that she could be trusted to do her job as prosecutor in Srebrenica within the limits of what she had?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You admit, do you not, that is just one person and not a judiciary, as you referred to her yesterday? For the record, that was page 61, line 1. That was one person doing the job of prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the steps which she took to have the jurisdiction of the High Court transferred to her, that wasn't some innovation of hers, but a step which the law contemplates, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she would have known that because she was a trained lawyer; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder -- I know it's a bit early but I wonder if I could take the break there. It's simply that I need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two minutes more and we have the break in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it normally 12:30? In that case could I have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And -- not much longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not much longer. So we will have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, one moment Mr. Jones until your client sits down and has hid headphones on. All right, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, Judge Tankic, just a few more questions. You spoke yesterday about the persons and organs which could report to the military prosecutor, talking about the district military prosecutor. Now do you agree that the military police or the security organ in a unit, the SVB, could refer a case directly to the district military Prosecutor without necessarily going through the unit commander?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, for example, an assistant commander for security in a brigade could refer a case to the military prosecutor without necessarily getting the approval of the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like you to guess your answer. I mean, if you know it, you know it. If you don't know it, just say so, please, because this is an important question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander is superior to these units, so he would have a role there, but I'm not sure about the military structure. I can't be precise in my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact you told us that the military prosecutor could receive information from any source? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I don't know if this is a helpful parallel or not, but I would like to read you a provision from the ICTY Statute referring to the powers of the prosecutor of this Tribunal and it's Article 18.1 of the Statute and it says, "The Prosecutor shall initiate investigations ex officio or on the basis of information obtained from any source". So would you agree that that is a power similar to the one you mentioned, namely, a prosecutor can obtain information from anyone?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is similar, but according to the formal law, we had the entire list of organs and persons and any citizen could file complaints so we are not talking about investigations. We are only talking about complaints being submitted to the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And essentially that is just a matter of common sense, isn't it, that a prosecutor can receive information from any source?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is according to the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now as far as you're awareness of cases in the nature of cases dealt with by the Srebrenica lower court is concerned, isn't your knowledge about those cases limited in the following respects and I'll go through them. Firstly, that you wouldn't know about court files which were left in Srebrenica when it fell to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw you nodding, but the interpreters need to hear your voice, near need to hear your answer. So please, if it is "da", say "da", if it's not, say not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't know about those cases, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could be, please be shown Exhibit P509 that's dated the 13th of November, 1995. I will just start reading the English any way. It says: "Criminal cases -- it refers to criminal cases that the basic public prosecutor's office in Srebrenica was dealing with until first of June 1993 were not handed over to the prosecutor and it is assumed they have been destroyed." So isn't it right also there may be criminal cases from before 1st of June 1993 which may have been destroyed from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you just quoted is a report of the higher prosecutor made according to the reports from the prosecutor in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And the higher prosecutor, there's the assumption there that cases might have been destroyed which dealt with the pre 1st of June 1993 period, doesn't she?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was a competent report of the prosecutor in Srebrenica. She was pretty precise when, in her report about the work in 1993, she said that there was -- that she found no ongoing case when she took her position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'm not sure if you're seeing the bit which I'm referring to. As I say, in English it says, "It's referring to criminal cases that the basic public prosecutor's office in Srebrenica was dealing with until 1993 were not handed over to the prosecutor and it is assumed that they have been destroyed". So that was really my question: Isn't it right that there may have been criminal cases, the files of which were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this follows from the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And you can keep that document with you because I'm going to turn to another section of it. But isn't your knowledge of cases which were sent to Tuzla also limited by the fact that you only reviewed the reports. You didn't actually go through the archives and look at each case file and so if there was any -- any case which did not appear in the reports, then you wouldn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as regarding the cases you've mentioned and this is just one more question on the Emir Halilovic case, can you confirm that Stojan Kersmanovic is the victim of a third murder was actually a Serb who was captured in Srebrenica and then was killed in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that third murder occurred in the hospital. I can't remember the name of the victim. I know that the first two murders were members of the Zekic family. I'm not sure about the name and surname of the third victim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But are you aware that the third victim was a Serb who had been captured and then taken to the hospital because he was injured?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that this was a Serb in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, staying with P509 for a moment, the date is the 13th of November 1995, so obviously after the fall of Srebrenica. Do you agree it was only after the fall and when Ms. Akagic was physically in Tuzla that it was possible to receive such detailed information about what had been going on in Srebrenica, that was the first time -- first time detailed information was received?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These information were provided by the prosecutor, Dzuzida Akagic, to the higher prosecutor, and she also reported orally about the situation in the basic prosecution office in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Once she was physically present in Tuzla, Ms. Akagic?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, as I mentioned earlier, there is a passage in this document which is only in the original but which I would like to get into the record. Since it is fairly lengthy, I don't propose that I try and read it. I wonder if I could ask the witness to read the passage, and then we will have the interpretation and it is all on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to that, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed that way then, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, the witness needs to know --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I will direct him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you in advance for your cooperation, Judge Tankic. If you would read the passage, it's on the first page and it's the last paragraph and it's the third sentence which starts: [B/C/S spoken]. If you could read from there just down to the end of that page, that would be very helpful, and slowly, if possible, so it can be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Due to the problems in acting in criminal cases falling under the jurisdiction of higher prosecution and district military prosecution, following the request by this prosecutor's office, the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina authorised Dzuzida Akagic, starting in January 1994, to carry out the duty of the High Public Prosecutor in criminal cases that fall under the jurisdiction of that prosecutor's office. "After the information by the district military court sent to the lower court in Srebrenica, numbered SU-127/94, dated 13th May 1994, this prosecutor's office and the public prosecutor's office of the republic submitted this prosecutor's office instructions on how to act in cases of most serious criminal offences falling under the jurisdiction of the district military prosecution to act in accordance with the Article 48 of the Criminal Proceedings Act."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to -- sorry, thank you. I'm going to pass up a new exhibit, which is a copy of Article 48 of the Criminal Procedure Code so that we can see what that's about. For the record, it is [B/C/S/ spoken] third amended edition, and we have a first copy of the cover page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Judge Tankic, if you could look at Article 48 of the Criminal Procedure Code, I will read the translation in English, which we have. It's an untranslation, it's our translation: "When there is the danger of delay, a public prosecutor lacking jurisdiction shall also undertake actions in the proceeding, but he or she must immediately inform the competent public prosecutor about it." Now, we've just seen in that document mention of Article 48, and it's a document from the Tuzla prosecutor, Vildana Helic. Isn't it right that, by referring to Article 48 there, it's clear that in Tuzla she still considers that Ms. Akagic was not the authorised person to conduct investigations and that therefore she could only function in accordance with Article 48?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But only when it came to military persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because she wasn't authorised otherwise to act -- to exercise jurisdiction over military persons?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have no further questions. I would ask for that document to be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be P216.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. D216.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D. I thank you, Mr. Jones. Correct, it is D, "D" for David, D216.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Ms. Sellers, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there will be a couple of points for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead and allow some time for us to put some questions too, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then the judge can go home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examined by Ms. Sellers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge Tankic, I will just ask a couple of questions. Would it be your opinion that, in August of 1992, if war crimes were to have been committed, that there would have been an obligation, therefore, to report such war crimes via any mechanism to the High Court in Tuzla who retained jurisdiction at that point?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The high prosecutor in Tuzla should have been informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it also be your testimony that if one were unaware that the district military court in Tuzla had been enacted and was functioning, that that person would continue to report any war crimes that might have been committed in the months of September or December or January to the high prosecutor's office in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, could one conclude that there would never be a jurisdictional lacuna or gap, particularly in the nature of crimes such as war crimes 141, 142, 143, 144, under the criminal statute, when it came to at least reporting these crimes and eventually prosecuting them?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, I do object to that question as being, A, leading and, B, trying to elicit opinion evidence by someone who isn't an expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge Tankic, was there a jurisdictional gap, meaning therefore lack of jurisdiction, during a certain time period as it pertained to war crimes under the Penal Code?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the territory of Srebrenica, therefore, always covered by some legal court and prosecutor's office that had jurisdiction over war crimes?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, apart from the objective difficulties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, exactly addressing some of those objective difficulties, the ability to convey information, would you see that as being different from the ability to ensure that a court proceeding, such as a trial, took place?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was blockade, they could only try to secure evidence and other things at the time and wait for a more favourable moment to report that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would those have been reasonable, reasonable means and steps to take in the absence of more -- a more facilitated manner of communication, when war crimes are --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again, that's asking for opinion evidence, whether it's reasonable or not. I don't think this witness is in a position to answer that sort of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge Tankic, as a judge, would proper steps have been to at least attempt to secure the crime scene, secure evidence, and secure the person before a prosecutor could take further steps of initiating an investigation?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge Tankic, prior to the establishment of the public prosecutor's office in Srebrenica in 1993, in June of 1993, would it, therefore, have been appropriate for any organ or any person who was aware that war crimes had been committed to keep paperwork, either in their own office or to convey them directly to the district military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't want to be objecting the whole time, but all of these questions are both leading and seeking to elicit evidence. If he's being asked -- if Judge Tankic is being asked what did the law provide, then that's fine. If he's being asked something which he has experience of, then that's fine. But it seems to be going to a string of questions, saying what would reasonable steps be. And apart from anything else, it is usurping Your Honours' function, with respect, as to what reasonable steps should be taken by someone in any given situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I thank you for your observation, and you notice -- you must have noticed that I upheld your previous objection, but this is somewhat different. This question, it's not a question of reasonableness, but it's a question of a legal assessment that the witness is being asked to make, I assume, on the basis of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, other words are being substituted, "proper" and "appropriate" for "reasonable", but none of the questions are actually asking, What did the law provide? And so this witness is going to give his evidence -- give opinion evidence about what would be reasonable steps for someone to take, and I don't see that he is qualified as an expert to give that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not being asked as an expert. He's being asked as a prosecutor at the time and a judge, also at the time, around about that time, whether this was a legal practice or not, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Provided he's sticking with what the law provides I don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I'm not upholding your objection, because otherwise I would have upheld that just as I did with the previous one. But here it is not a question of making an assessment as to whether it is reasonable or not. It's a question of whether this would be legal or whether it will be outside the parameters of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So be it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. Do you want to repeat the question, Ms. Sellers, because by now we have lost the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, I would just like to see the transcript again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge Tankic, I asked you would it be the proper steps, under what would be legal and proper steps therefore to secure the crime scene, secure the evidence and secure the person if they had known that war crimes had been committed before a prosecutor could take further steps at the initiating of an investigation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I understand now that it's the subsequent question, if I could just state that. It's Judge Tankic, prior to the establishment of the public prosecutor's office in Srebrenica in 1993, in June of 1993, would it therefore have been appropriate for any organ or any person who is aware that war crimes had been committed to keep paperwork either in their own office or to convey them directly to the district military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And by -- and by appropriate, please understand legally permissible or lawful, and don't go beyond that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We must distinguish between a complaint on the one hand and evidence on the other. Anyone could have filed a complaint. As for securing any evidence, only authorised personnel would have been authorised to do that sort of thing; the civilian police, the military police, bodies of law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Judge Tankic, even though it appears that prolonged detention was problematic in Srebrenica, did that obviate the obligation of commanders or persons in positions of responsibility from at least detaining someone for 15 days if they had committed war crimes?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As concerns detention, if you look at the law on criminal procedure, only an investigating magistrate can order detention, or later a trial chamber may as well order detention, but that is at a later stage. Under the military rules, I believe it's slightly different, but I don't have any specific knowledge of that that would enable me to answer your question. I do know, however, that under the law on criminal procedure, that was adopted, a commander was under an obligation to secure all evidence to detain the perpetrator, to secure the crime scene until a prosecutor was informed. This is an explicit obligation under the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Tankic, right now I'm -- Your Honour, as Defence counsel, I draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit P497. Similar to what Defence counsel did, I will read out the pertinent part in order to save a bit of time. This has already been entered as an exhibit. I would like to draw attention to Article 27, that says: "The military commander or the military unit institution is obliged to inform immediately the district military prosecutor or supreme commander about the information referred to in paragraph 1". Paragraph 1 talks about the commander of the unit and securing a person who committed criminal acts for which official prosecution is foreseen. Judge Tankic, would you agree that in the absence of being able to directly inform the district military prosecutor that the military commander then had the option of informing the supreme commander according to the statutory order on district military courts?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would also, within the same document, like to draw your attention to Article 29. At the end of Article 29, it says that: "If the military commander or the authorised official person is not able to do so", referring to detention, "he is immediately", latest within 8 hours, "obliged to inform an examining magistrate of the district military court or the nearest military unit or institution which shall take the prisoner to the examined magistrate of the district military court". And Judge Tankic, my question: Is it foreseen within the law, these exceptional circumstances or alternative circumstances in terms of detention for military commanders?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just a few questions left. I would like Prosecution Exhibit P46 to be placed on Sanctions. I believe that we can look at it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't believe I referred to P46 in my cross-examination. I wonder if this arises from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what the question is going to be and what prompts Ms. Sellers to refer to P46. I haven't got a clue, as yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can certainly make a proffer of evidence. Defence counsel did spend quite a bit of time on the lack of knowledge, within the enclave of Srebrenica, concerning the district military court, the non-arrival of gazettes or of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's cut it short. What do you purport to prove by reference to P46?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: My reference to P46 I would like to show that certainly not only was the existence of a district military court known, security organs knew it and they were -- they have produced documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But they refer to the military High Court in that document, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't seen the document. Let's see -- let's see what the question is, Mr. Jones. I think it does arise out of your cross-examination, but at least to -- I would say to a large extent I would say. Let's proceed. Is the document on Sanction or...

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It is. Mr. Tankic, I would ask you to look at document P46, which you have seen before, and, once again, I would ask: Do you consider the last sentence in this document to be reference to the district military court or referred to a military institution that was capable of taking crimes alleged to have been committed by certain persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now that I've heard the question, I do object because he was asked that exact question in examination-in-chief and again it's the same problem here is written military High Court and he is being asked to -- he is being asked for the second time to say that that is the Tuzla district military court when he doesn't know. He's not the author.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was covered during your examination-in-chief, with documents -- other documents that used exactly the same terminology.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's skip to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the next question, Your Honour, would consider the third murder in the hospital that could have fallen under, according to Defence, an article that pertained to war crimes. I ask you, Judge Tankic, therefore would you -- assuming that this crime did fall under war crimes, would you therefore be in a position to state that authorities in Srebrenica were aware of the existence that war crimes could be tried?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question, Judge. Next question, Ms. Sellers. I didn't allow -- I didn't allow Mr. Jones to proceed with that line of questioning when it came -- when it came to that matter. So why take it up as if I hadn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, my final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- taken any steps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: My final question is: Judge Tankic, would you agree that any manner of bringing a complaint of the district military office or conveying information, would not be dependent, legally, on the extent of functioning of a district military office once it had jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge Tankic, is the legal obligation to report criminal information to the district military court based upon or dependent upon the extent of that court's functioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's under Bosnian law -- I hope, otherwise, Your Honour, he's being asked questions about the ultimate issue which Your Honours will have to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Let's say under the statutory law from Bosnia that we have seen and the law within the gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You would be opening a Pandora's box because the next question I would ask -- would the principle of impossibility apply under Bosnian law. Come on, let's leave it at that Ms. Sellers. Please, because you can't expect that much from the witness -- but not too much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay, certainly. I'll withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do you have any -- and do you have any. Yes, Judge, we have almost finished. Our practice here is that the Bench, if there are some questions for you, will do that, will -- Judge Brydensholt has got a question for you. Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: I understand that according to the laws which were in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, 1993, it was right for everybody to submit a complaint, a report to the prosecution office. But I think you also said that it was an obligation, it was not only something which everybody would have the power to do, but it was even an obligation. Is that rightly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And among those institutions which were under such an obligation, I think you mentioned also a hospital as a public institution. So if a hospital would see that a person had been violated seriously, they would be under an obligation to report that, is that rightly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't have any questions either, Judge, which means that we have come to an end, to the end of your testimony. Judge Tankic, I would like to thank you on my own behalf, on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and on behalf of Judge Eser but also on behalf of the Tribunal for having been so kind as to come over and give testimony in this case against Naser Oric. You will soon be escorted out of the courtroom by our usher, who will ensure together with the rest of the stuff that you receive all of the attention and the assistance you require to enable your return back home at the earliest possible -- at the earliest possible. On my own behalf, but also on behalf of everyone present here in this courtroom, I should also like to wish you a safe journey back home. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will resume on Monday and that is in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was just going to say that on that occasion I should be joined by my lead counsel, but I think it is one of those occasions when those of Islamic faith say "inshallah".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
